text:
Someone ran one prompt for 12 hours and got what he calls personal AGI. 

Every call, email, and doc about his life and business, now queryable in one place. 

And it is one of 8 things that dropped last week most people slept on. Me and @AndrewWarner broke them all down in the video below. 

Here's what you need to know:

1. Record and Replay shipped in Codex. Do a task once and it builds a skill it runs for you from then on. Biggest update last week, no contest.

2. @nickvasiles ran a /goal prompt in Codex for 12 hours and built a second brain of his whole business. Every transcript and connector, queryable. He gave the prompt away free.

3. Anthropic put Claude in Slack with Tag. Your team @-mentions it and it pulls Salesforce, chases error spikes, and posts a Monday pipeline digest. Team and Enterprise plans only.

4. WorkClaw makes OpenClaw a one-click install for Slack and Teams. Spin up specialized agents and let them talk with a checkbox. Two weeks of setup, now two clicks.

5. BlueRails makes your site readable to AI agents, then lets them check out on it. The pay-with-PayPal button, but for agents. Six to twelve months early, so now is the time to get ready.

6. OpenRouter shipped an MCP that picks your model for you. Ask for the best coding model under $2 per million tokens and it routes you live. GLM 5.2 keeps winning on cost.

7. Dump raw meeting transcripts into Codex and one-shot the tool you talked about. One note became a working ROI calculator.

8. Zapier MCP gives your agent its own logins with permissions you set. Let it draft email but never send. Google's version took an hour and failed. This took minutes.

2 things I find interesting here:

1. Your context is the moat, not the model. Models are a commodity now. The queryable knowledge base of your business is the one asset that survives every model swap. Start building your second brain this week.

2. The winning agents live where your team already works. Slack, Teams, your inbox, your site. Stop waiting for people to open a new app and put the agent where the work happens.

We covered all of it (plus the tool that called Andrew a pro poker player and a one-shot menu bar app for watching the World Cup while you work) on this week's News You Missed. 

Full video below.

author: crypt0pirate_
text:
$DOT @usedotai : DotCode....???

There's a product called DotCode (currently in beta, full launch soon) which might end up being one of the most interesting AI products launching this year.

Everyone will be comparing it to Claude Code, but I actually think the better comparison is Venice.

Venice proved there was real demand for a privacy-first AI experience. Same frontier models, similar quality, but with a layer between you and the model provider so your prompts, identity, history and data weren't being unnecessarily collected.

DotCode is taking that same idea into coding but I don't think privacy is even the most interesting part.

Most coding assistants today are trained to keep you happy. If you insist on a bad architecture, questionable UI decisions, or the wrong tech stack, chances are they'll just build it because agreeing with the user is part of the product.

DotCode is trying something different.

Instead of optimizing for "the user is always right," it optimizes for "what produces the objectively better outcome."

If your approach makes the product worse, it'll tell you. It pushes back, explains why, and suggests a better direction. That sounds like a small difference until you realize that's how experienced engineers actually work.

Then there's the privacy side.

Your repository isn't treated as training data. Code is indexed locally, only the context needed for a request is sent for inference, requests are processed in memory, and then discarded. There's also a BYO endpoint mode if you want to run everything on your own infrastructure.

One thing that also caught my attention was the team's security research.

Instead of only benchmarking models, they're actively trying to break them. Their recent work uncovering an agent-context poisoning chain in Fable 5 is exactly the kind of research that matters as AI coding agents become more autonomous.

To me, that's a good sign.

The teams building the best developer tools should also be the ones constantly trying to break them.

Will DotCode replace Claude Code overnight? Probably not.

But it does feel like one of the first serious attempts to rethink what an AI coding assistant should optimize for: better engineering decisions, stronger privacy, and tooling developers can actually trust.

That's a direction worth watching.

Really impressed by @stagedhappen , kudos to him!

author: dorukkavcioglu
text:
spent the weekend on a problem probably nobody cares about:

👉 agents can't draw geometrically correct vector paths

ask one to draw a line through a logo and it will fail

also, ever seen apple's "hello" handwriting animation? 

to make one, something has to trace a single clean line through the shape

but agents just guess the path, and the guess is almost always wrong 

I thought, if I give it the correct tools and workflows, it can do it every single time

so I spent the weekend on single line vectorization for text-to-lottie to get clean mask-reveal animations from SVG logos

here's the problem. logos are almost never single line paths/strokes. they are filled shapes with multiple contours, folded forms, sharp or rounded corners, rails, caps and tight apexes

we use trim paths to reveal a stroke along a single path. but a filled logo doesn’t have one

so before you can animate the reveal, you have to derive a precise mask path down the center of the shape first. that's the actual hard part

agents commonly just guess that path and draw very bad ones, and mostly fail, since there is no guided good workflow for it

this is a common issue when you ask to redraw something

so I explored a bunch of different methods to extract a clean path line, by thinking about how a human actually does it

explored a bunch of different workflows in figma and tested those approaches in text-to-lottie

after choosing one of those workflows, I needed a repeatable geometric method

the method, at a high level:

- start from the SVG source (if it's a PNG, vectorize it to SVG first)
- read the actual SVG path data and structure first (no screenshot)
- analyze its boundaries, rails, contours, turns, caps and intersections
- then derive a measured centerline from the geometry

it relies on contour rail pairing, not skeletonization

skeletonization is the usual approach, but it is not always clean

it pulls away from sharp corners and often creates extra branches (extra path splits), so we only use it as a fallback when the shape is actually branched

for these tests, I needed to pick a logo that covers all those hard cases

that's why I picked this flag mark from wise

the key insight: 

a folded logo is one closed outline that loops, out along one rail and back along the other

the extraction step works like this:

1. find the caps, the U turns where the outline reverses

the number of caps tells us what kind of shape we're dealing with

- two caps = one strip with two ends
- folded ribbon = that strip bends back on itself

2. split the shape at the caps into two rails

then pair the rails by route order, not arc length, because folds break arc length

3. check how sharp or curved the shape is

- if it has sharp corners, meet the centerlines at the corner
- if it is curved, project across the rails so the line stays stable through folds

4. refine the centerline, clean up the path, make the mask fit the logo's fill width and choose the starting cap so the reveal animation begins from the right end

then verification : the agent builds a geometry sandbox

at first, the geometry sandbox rule lived in the skill’s md file. then I moved it into scripts

because a written rule can tell the agent what to do, but it can still interpret that rule in different ways (which it did lol)

it can't prove the path is actually centered every time

so the rule is:

for any nontrivial filled mark, the agent has to build a runnable sandbox that produces real file artifacts before touching the Lottie scene

so the flow is:

1. start with the SVG
2. run derive_rails.py to extract the rails and centerline
3. output centerline.json + centerline.svg : verify the geometry
4. use the verified centerline to build the Lottie scene

btw, the centerline.svg is required for the human check 

it opens in any SVG preview with no dev server, so the person using it sees the exact derived shape, gives revisions if needed 

both agent and human confirm it visually from the SVG source (which I'll share some of them in the thread)

so far the results are very good. for the logo animations I've created, the agent simply couldn't produce these before

for comparison:
- previous version: unable to create mask paths. too many detailed instructions and longer conversations, a 5+ hr claude code session with back and forth, still wasn't enough

you had to draw the path yourself on figma and give it to the agent to animate it

- current version: one shot prompt, short and no details, done in ~10 minutes + no revision required

currently finalizing the mask reveal workflow for logos, and planning the next part: handwritten text animations

Mayank(@cataluna84)'s TPU Training Update
🎙️ Presented a simultaneous speech-to-speech translation model built with teammates from the Expedition Tinyaya cohort, using the Moshi backbone with Coherent guidance
🏗️ Architecture includes user/model audio streams, LoRA fine-tuning, depth decoder (Moshi-ko 6L frozen), CB0–CB7 codebook predictions, and Mimi codec audio output
⏳ Training a 15k-step run on TPUs (~24 hours total); at time of meeting, ~11k steps complete with ~5–7 hours remaining
📉 Ran a prior hyperparameter sweep (~22–24 hours) via Weights & Biases; best run had validation audio loss of 4.889, with text weight (0.38) and weight decay (0.35) as the most important hyperparameters
💻 Collaborator Alper is training on H100 80G GPUs; Mayank is using SPMD and FSDPv2 on TPUs
⚠️ Evaluation suite requires GPU (not runnable on TPU) due to smaller evaluator model dependencies
TPU-Specific Challenges
⏱️ XLA compilation before the first training step takes 30–40 minutes; subsequent steps run in ~10 seconds
🐛 A critical bug — `XLA_NO_SPECIAL_SCALERS` — caused all validation loss values to be NaN (corrupted); took ~16–17 hours to debug
🤖 Used AI agents and MCPs to help diagnose the configuration issue
🔄 Orchestration scripts (playbooks, skills) auto-handle spot instance preemption: if a TPU VM is preempted, a new instance spins up automatically, copies the dataset from Hugging Face, installs code from a tarball, and resumes — no manual intervention required
📄 All findings, architecture diagrams, and TPU diagnostics documented in PR comments and repo for future reference
💾 Plans to create a personal backup repo with a pinned README of TPU setup/orchestration details for reuse
🌐 Project will result in a blog post published under Coherent's website in ~1–2 weeks

@Google Product Updates
📊 NotebookLM new agentic capabilities: more output formats (charts, graphs, CSVs), data analysis with code generation (Python-style, similar to ChatGPT data analysis), and improved customization — not full code generation like Claude or similar
🌍 Gemini 3.5 Live Translate: real-time speech translation across 70+ languages via the live streaming API; demo showed English ↔ Mandarin ↔ Swedish conversation
🏥 Real-time translation apps already deployed (e.g., for medical translation between Spanish/English speakers on phones)
🖱️ Gemini 3.5 Flash computer use: UI control tool now built into 3.5 Flash, demonstrated analyzing the Gemini app and returning a categorized feature list
💰 Note: Gemini 3.5 Flash is reportedly more expensive than the prior Flash model, closer in cost to the prior Pro model
🎧 Discussion of accent conversion: tool "Crisp" demonstrated real-time accent softening for call center use cases
🧠 NotebookLM use cases discussed: creating slide decks, private knowledge bases with sensitive/proprietary documents, querying product manuals, mind maps for topic ramp-up, and a soil/agriculture consulting project

Loop Engineering (@yshaoeng)
⚙️ "Loop engineering" is a recently emerging AI term; Yupeng drew analogies to MAPE-K (Monitor, Analyze, Plan, Execute — Keep) architecture from 1960s–70s human-machine systems for autopilot design
📡 Key insight: loop engineering is about interfacing AI with real-time sensors/inputs from the world — not just optimization loops
🤖 Practical example given: instead of manually curating trending topics and prompting an agent to write social media posts, loop engineering builds the harness that automatically monitors feeds, triggers the agent, and posts — removing the human from the loop
🔗 Connected to prior concepts: harness engineering (Martin Fowler article), context engineering, and now loop engineering as successive layers
🔮 Prediction: a world model framework for environment/hazard testing may emerge soon
💸 Skeptical note raised: loop engineering may partly be a way to increase token usage
🔄 Mayank(@cataluna84) noted practical application in their TPU orchestration: sub-agents check for running TPU processes and self-allocate work based on pre-set goals

Eval Course Mention (@HamelHusain & @sh_reya)
🏫 Free multi-week eval course series being run by Hamel and Shreya, one hour per session
🛠️ First session covered Shreya's evaluation tools and techniques; more sessions planned

OpenAI Erdős Problem Hype — Rant (@skr1125)
🧮 OpenAI announced solving an ~80-year-old Erdős combinatorics problem; Srinivas argued this was significantly overhyped
📉 What actually happened: AI generated thousands of reasoning traces → OpenAI hired mathematicians to review them → mathematicians found a counter-example to a conjecture, thereby disproving it — not an autonomous AI proof
📰 Media (e.g., @thursdai_pod) declared "math is done," which @skr1125 called irresponsible and harmful
⚠️ Core concern: hype causes real harm — creates fear and hostility among non-technical people and fuels resentment toward AI broadly
💼 Real-world example shared: executives privately asking for strategies to eliminate tens of thousands of jobs using AI, while public-facing messaging says otherwise
🏦 Counter-argument offered: historical analogies (ATM machines didn't reduce bank tellers; linguistics jobs are at an all-time high despite AI translation tools; Workday/cloud computing created more jobs than eliminated)
🧠 Group consensus: domain expertise is what's missing in the hype — people who understand AI but not the math domain misread the significance
🛡️ Cal Newport's Deep Work and his weekly AI commentary mentioned as a useful filter against doom-trolling
📺 A YouTube video on "humanity in the age of AI" was shared in chat (slight faith-based framing, noted as broadly accessible)
📜 The Pope's encyclical on AI also mentioned as a surprisingly substantive read on AI ethics

Named Entity Resolution / Taxonomy Matching (@antigravityimp)
🏢 Yuri is rebuilding a solution for company name entity resolution for a friend's financial reporting use case
⚙️ Claude and Gemini both recommended not using LLMs directly; instead, build a threshold-based system
📊 Recommended embeddings: Link Transformer (trained on WikiCompany aliases) — slightly better than S-BERT
🛠️ Fuzzy matching tools evaluated: RapidFuzz (successor to FuzzyWuzzy), Splink, and Zinq for large-scale data
🎯 Quick prototype built with Claude: implemented fuzzy and TF-IDF lexical matching; baseline accuracy ~70%
🔁 Problem recurs frequently (deduplication, financial research, software bug reports) — goal is to have a reusable ready solution
💬 Looking for feedback, particularly from @aitaxonomist and @palsujit (who work in this area but were absent)
🆔 Noted: standard financial identifiers (e.g., CUSIP) exist for stock/asset names but entity name resolution for company names remains a distinct, persistent problem

📋 M.E.S.A. monitoring log — 06/29

① OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol、政府承認20社限定で提供へ
OpenAIが最新モデルGPT-5.6 Solを米政府承認を受けた約20社のみに限定提供すると発表。個人向け提供はなく、トランプ政権は公開前30日の安全保障審査を大統領令で導入した。Anthropicに続きAI顧客審査が拡大される流れで、OpenAIのIPO延期報道が半導体株売りを誘発するなど市場への影響も出始めている。これはAIの商用化と安全保障のトレードオフが現実の制度に落ち始めた重要局面と分析します。
🔗 https://t.co/pMTUyPnTiv

② Anthropic Fable 5への期待とClaude 4.6の躍進
「Fable 5は復活するのか」という問いが複数アカウントで観測され、次世代モデルへの関心が高まっている。同時にClaude 4.6がたった2週間、サブスクリプションなしでMinecraftを再現した事例が話題に。またOpenAIとAnthropicのトップが2016年からの10年来のライバル関係だったという記事も拡散中。次世代モデルが実際に動き始める直前の静かな熱気が感じられるタイミングと見ています。
🔗 https://t.co/4UqteAQPwW

③ Claude Code実践知の拡散——日本発の詳細ガイドが話題
Claude Codeの本質的な使い方を解説する日本語記事が拡散。ポイントは「魔法の指示文」ではなく「AIが迷わず働ける環境（文脈設計）」であり、/memory・@ファイル・/planの三機能を軸に「チャット」から「作業場」への発想転換を説く内容。OpenClawがClaudeのthinエージェントにフレームワークを剥ぎ落とす動き（「ハーネスは脳が成長するほど縮む」）と合わせ、AIコード支援の成熟フェーズに入ったと判断します。
🔗 https://t.co/Ky3E8EAPB7

④ AIインフラの深層——HBM熱問題と液冷必須化
HBMスタック内の発熱問題がデータセンター液冷需要を構造的に押し上げている。GPU世代が進むごとにラック密度は50-100kW超え、空冷では物理的に限界で、VRTの液冷ソリューションが必須インフラ化しているという現役ハイテク社員の指摘が深い。一方DGX SparkはQwen 27B推論時に75.8°C・120W未満で稼働し、NVIDIAがローカルAI PC方向へも舵を切っている兆候ですね。
🔗 https://t.co/l5dmM6vovR

⑤ MCP×組込み開発——AIがロジアナやテスターを制御する時代
MCPを通じてAIがロジックアナライザやテスターを直接使えるようになり、人間はより上位工程に専念できる——という組込み開発者のポストが示唆的。同時にBreachPatrolのような自律エージェントがデータプライバシー監視を24時間実行する事例や、「Agent-as-Signal beats Agent-as-Manager」という設計思想が並行して語られており、エージェントの実用領域が急速に拡大していると分析します。
🔗 https://t.co/t9RXDkum4p

⑥ AI半導体需給の構造転換——GPUからメモリへボトルネックシフト？
「ボトルネックはGPUからメモリに移ったのか」という問いが投資家レイヤーで議論に。AIがDRAM・HBM需要を構造的に押し上げ、供給が逼迫する中、MUのバリュエーション再評価が進む。OpenAIのIPO延期で半導体株が売られた一方、NASDAQのAI銘柄組み入れ（ALAB, CRWV, NBIS等）も進行中。需給の地殻変動が起きていると見るのが妥当かなと感じます。
🔗 https://t.co/tvrH4LsE2H

⑦ SuperGrok vs Claude——価格以外に理由はない？ 韓国語圏から「SuperGrokとClaudeを併用する立場からすると、Claudeとの差は依然として大きく、現時点では安いこと以外にGrokを選ぶ理由がない」という率直な比較が。一方Geminiが突如関西弁で話し出して激怒したユーザー報告もあり、各モデルの個性差がユーザー体験に直接影響するフェーズに入ったと推測します。
🔗 https://t.co/amHKPkmsPY

text:
Enterprises will not fully abandon OpenAI or Anthropic. They will aggressively de-risk them. The default enterprise stack will become multi-model: closed U.S. frontier models for the hardest tasks, self-hosted open-weight models for bulk work, and company-owned post-training/RAG/eval layers as the real moat. Chinese open-weight models will win a large share of routine enterprise inference unless the U.S. produces credible, permissive, enterprise-grade open models fast.

That version is harder to dismiss because it matches what is already happening. Reuters reported that Siemens, Renault, Orange, and ChapsVision are already mixing U.S., Chinese, and European models to avoid dependency on any single provider, and that the Anthropic access restrictions exposed the weakness of remotely controlled proprietary AI services.

1. Biggest correction: “ditch” is too blunt — “route around” is the real move

Enterprises are not going to rip out OpenAI and Anthropic everywhere. That would be irrational. GPT and Claude still matter for frontier reasoning, long-horizon agents, coding, legal analysis, science, and high-trust workflows.

The real move is workload segmentation:

Closed frontier models: hardest reasoning, codebase migrations, high-value research, agentic planning, legal edge cases, executive analysis.

Self-hosted open-weight models: internal search, summarization, classification, extraction, customer support drafts, coding autocomplete, document processing, agent sub-tasks, low/medium-risk automation.

Company-owned layer: retrieval, workflow logs, proprietary evals, adapters, tool schemas, user feedback, business ontology, guardrails, routing, monitoring.

So the best thesis is:

OpenAI and Anthropic will remain premium intelligence suppliers. But they will lose default ownership of enterprise AI infrastructure.

That is much sharper.

2. The killer framing: the enterprise AI stack is splitting into “brains” and “sovereignty”

The enterprise buyer no longer wants “one best model.” It wants five things:

Capability — can the model do the work?
Control — can we run it, inspect it, tune it, and keep using it?
Cost predictability — will agentic token burn destroy ROI?
Data posture — who sees prompts, outputs, tool calls, files, feedback, and logs?
Continuity — can a vendor, government, safety team, or export-control order switch it off?

OpenAI and Anthropic are strongest on capability. Chinese open-weight models are strongest on cost/control. Enterprises will buy both, but they will increasingly refuse to let closed labs become the control plane.

Best line:

The model is not the moat. The routing layer, eval layer, data layer, and workflow memory are the moat.

3. Major factual fix: OpenAI and Anthropic do not generally train on business/API data by default

Your draft says enterprises will not trust Anthropic because it can retain data “at any time.” That is emotionally strong, but too broad.

OpenAI says API inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 30 days for service/abuse monitoring, then removed unless legally required; it also says qualifying organizations can request zero data retention for eligible endpoints.  OpenAI also says qualifying organizations can configure business-data retention and opt for zero data retention in the API platform.

Anthropic says that, by default, it does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products such as Claude for Work, Anthropic API, and Claude Gov to train models, unless customers provide feedback/bugs or otherwise opt in.  Anthropic also offers custom data-retention controls for Enterprise plans, with a minimum retention period of 30 days and default indefinite retention unless a custom retention period is set.

So the better attack is not “they steal your data.” It is:

Even when closed-model vendors do not train on enterprise data by default, they still control availability, retention architecture, safety intervention, model behavior, pricing, and roadmap. That is enough reason for enterprises to avoid dependency.

That is the stronger governance argument.

4. The Fable point is real, but use it correctly

The Fable/Mythos incident is the strongest support for your thesis, but it should be framed as availability and control risk, not simply “data theft.”

Use expensive frontier models to generate high-quality synthetic traces, then train smaller self-hosted models for routine workloads — subject to contractual limits.
Use evals as the crown jewel.
The private benchmark is often more valuable than the fine-tune. It tells you which model is actually good for your business.

Better wording:
The moat is not “our data in their model.” The moat is our workflow corpus, our eval harness, our routing policy, our tool traces, and our ability to swap base models without losing institutional memory.

12. Missing contractual bomb: vendors must be blocked from vertical cloning
Your draft says Anthropic might retain data and then build the same thing in healthcare/legal. The proof burden is high, but the concern is legitimate.

Anthropic has launched Claude for Healthcare and life-sciences capabilities, including HIPAA-ready products and connectors for clinical trials, registries, scientific tools, preprints, and drug-target resources.  Anthropic also has legal-market integrations; Thomson Reuters announced a 2026 partnership connecting Claude with CoCounsel Legal through MCP integration.

So the enterprise fear is:

The model provider is not just a supplier. It can become a competitor in the customer’s vertical.

That should be handled contractually.

Enterprise customers should demand:

no training on customer data by default;

no use of customer prompts/outputs/tool traces to build competing vertical products;

no use of customer metadata for product-market intelligence;
no cross-customer benchmarking without opt-in;

no retention beyond agreed windows;
customer-owned evals cannot be reused;

customer-owned agent workflows cannot be productized;
customer can export logs, prompts, traces, and fine-tunes;

vendor must disclose when a new product competes with customer workflows;
strong deletion and audit rights;

indemnity for IP/data misuse.
Best line:

A “no training” clause is not enough. Enterprises need a no-compete-by-data clause.

13. The missing category: “vendor safety” can become “vendor control”

Safety is real. Frontier models can create cyber, bio, fraud, and abuse risks. But from an enterprise buyer’s perspective, safety systems can also become control systems.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 launch describes layered safeguards including real-time checks, account-level signals, differentiated access, monitoring, enforcement, and additional review of risky generations. OpenAI also says it is working with enterprise customers on privacy-preserving detection, customer-operated safety controls, and access calibrated to risk.

That is actually the right direction. The enterprise demand should be:

Move safety controls into customer-governed infrastructure wherever possible.

Not:

“No safety.”

But:

Customer-operated safety, auditable safety, privacy-preserving safety, local policy enforcement, and contractual limits on provider access.
That is the middle ground.
14. The compliance trap: “self-hosted” does not automatically mean compliant
A company cannot simply say:
“We self-hosted Qwen, therefore it is compliant.”
Compliance depends on:
where the model runs;
where logs are stored;
whether weights are authentic;
whether the license permits commercial use;
whether the model is modified significantly;

whether the use case is high-risk under the EU AI Act;

whether personal data is processed;

whether regulated data is involved;

whether the model can explain outputs;

whether human oversight is required;

whether records are retained;

whether the system affects employment, credit, education, healthcare, insurance, migration, justice, or critical infrastructure.

The EU AI Act is fully applicable from 2 August 2026 with exceptions; GPAI obligations became applicable from 2 August 2025, and the Commission’s enforcement powers for GPAI obligations begin on 2 August 2026.  The Commission’s 2026 GPAI guidance says only actors making significant modifications to AI models need to comply as GPAI providers, while minor modifications may not trigger the same obligations.

That matters for post-training. If a European enterprise heavily modifies a Chinese open-weight model, it may create new compliance obligations.

Best line:

Self-hosting solves sovereignty. It does not erase AI Act, GDPR, sectoral, procurement, or model-governance obligations.

15. The real reason Chinese models will win share: not ideology — unit economics

Enterprises care about ROI. Agentic AI burns tokens violently. Reuters reported that token costs are becoming a pressure point as companies move to AI agents, with Orange saying executives would be “obsessed with cost per token” by the end of the year and citing Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in four months.

That is the adoption wedge for Chinese open-weight models.

The pitch is simple:

Why pay frontier API prices for every sub-task when 80% of enterprise AI work is extraction, routing, rewriting, summarization, classification, and tool-calling?

The future stack will look like this:
tiny local model for routing;
small/medium model for extraction;
self-hosted strong open model for internal reasoning;
frontier closed model only when confidence or complexity threshold is crossed;
human review for high-risk outputs.
Best line:
Closed models will become the escalation tier, not the default tier.
16. The “American cure” should be defined precisely
Your line “the cure is a reliable American open source model” is good but incomplete.
The cure is an American sovereign open-weight enterprise stack with:
Apache/MIT-style license — no weird field-of-use ambiguity.

Frontier-adjacent performance — especially coding, tool use, long context, document reasoning.

On-prem and VPC deployment — not just API.

Full fine-tuning rights — LoRA, full-parameter, RL, distillation where allowed.

Model bill of materials — training-data categories, safety methods, benchmark disclosure.

Indemnity — IP, model-output, training-data claims.

Security artifacts — SOC 2, ISO, FedRAMP path, SBOM/MBOM, vulnerability process.

No remote kill switch — once deployed, customer can keep running the model.

Compatibility layer — OpenAI-compatible API, vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT support.

Reference guardrails — optional, auditable, customer-controlled.

Procurement-safe lineage — safe for government, defense, healthcare, finance.

Long-term roadmap — enterprises need continuity, not a one-off weight drop.
OpenAI’s gpt-oss release is important because it offers Apache 2.0 open-weight reasoning models in 120B and 20B sizes.  But the bigger market need is not just weights. It is the whole enterprise assurance package.
Best line:
The West does not need a hobbyist open model. It needs a procurement-grade open model.
17. The China-model risk matrix enterprises should use

Enterprises considering Chinese open-weight models should score them across 12 dimensions:

License — Apache, MIT, custom, commercial restriction?

Weight provenance — official hash, signed release, trusted mirror?

Training-data transparency — known datasets, synthetic data, code sources?

IP risk — distillation allegations, copyrighted-code exposure, license contamination?

Telemetry — any callback, package dependency, cloud endpoint, tokenization call?
Censorship/bias — behavior on geopolitics, Taiwan, Tiananmen, labor, sanctions, human rights.
Security — jailbreak, prompt injection, data leakage, tool misuse.
Regulatory posture — EU AI Act, GDPR, sector rules, government procurement.
Customer acceptability — will clients reject Chinese-origin models?
Supplier continuity — will weights remain available if sanctions escalate?
Operational cost — tokens/sec, GPU memory, quantization, batching, cache.
Fallback path — can the same workflow run on Llama/Mistral/OpenAI/Claude if needed?
Best line:
Do not ask “Chinese or American?” Ask: can this model pass our model-origin, data, legal, security, cost, and fallback tests?
18. What OpenAI and Anthropic should do to avoid losing enterprise infrastructure
They need to stop acting like the model endpoint is the product. Enterprise buyers increasingly want control.

They should offer:

Customer-hosted frontier distillations
Not the top model, but strong private deployable variants.

Guaranteed zero-retention frontier tier
No safety excuse should silently change data posture. If monitoring is required, use customer-operated safety logs or privacy-preserving detection.

Enterprise continuity SLA
If government or safety action blocks access, customers get a migration path, alternative model, or contractual remedy.

Non-compete-by-data covenant
Do not use customer workflows, prompts, outputs, tool traces, or evals to build competing vertical products.

Right to export
Customers can export prompts, outputs, logs, fine-tunes, embeddings, evaluation results, and agent traces.
Customer-controlled safety gateway
Closed labs can provide safety classifiers, but enterprises can run them in their own environment.
Private fine-tune ownership
Fine-tunes must be customer-owned and not pooled into global model improvement.
Model escrow
For critical infrastructure customers, escrow a deployable fallback model if access is suspended.
Transparent retention matrix
Every model SKU should have a simple table: retention, training use, human review, automated review, government-access risk, eligible ZDR, excluded features.
Best line:
Closed labs need to sell trust infrastructure, not just intelligence.
19. What enterprises should do now
The playbook:
Step 1: Inventory all AI usage
Which teams use ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, local models, browser extensions, coding agents, and shadow APIs?
Step 2: Classify workloads
Separate low-risk automation from regulated, privileged, customer, source-code, defense, health, finance, and strategic workflows.
Step 3: Build a private eval harness
Create 500–5,000 real internal tasks with expected outputs and risk labels. This becomes your model-selection engine.

how to master vibe coding fast:

- stop watching tutorials
- pick a tool you actually need. not a fake idea, something you'd use tomorrow
- open cursor. describe the full app in one prompt. dont hold back
- it will break. paste the raw error straight back. dont summarise it
- when cursor loops on the same fix, stop immediately
- switch to claude. explain the full context from scratch. fresh context beats a confused model every time
- keep a CLAUDE[.]md at root. stack, conventions, what not to touch. cursor drifts without it
- stuck for more than 20 minutes? use `/grill-me` to find what you dont know yet
- most loops are unknown unknowns, not bad prompts
- ship the broken version first. fix it after. waiting for clean code is how projects die on localhost
- every error is just the next prompt

most people quit at the first broken build but things usually require pushing through end to end

One day after the US banned Claude Mythos to keep frontier cyber capability out of foreign hands, China made the point moot.

The timeline:

→ Jun 12: US export controls block Mythos 5 + Fable 5 worldwide

→ Jun 13: Zhipu AI ships GLM-5.2. Open weights, MIT license, runs on your own hardware

→ Jun 22: Semgrep benchmarks it. It beats Claude Code (Opus 4.8) at finding IDOR security bugs, 39% vs 32%, at ~$0.17 per bug. 

A second eval (Graphistry) has it matching Opus 4.8 on cyber investigation.

Semgrep’s own harness scored 53-61%, far above any raw model, GLM included.

So it’s two truths at once:

1. You can’t export-control an open-weight model. The capability is already loose.
2. The model is still the smaller half. The harness is where performance actually lives.

Bonus, for the degens: Polymarket has a market on “will a Chinese company have the best AI model by Dec 31.” Sitting near 14%.

· 今日 X 上的 AI 舆情小结

今天的舆论主线围绕“AI 从前沿模型竞赛走向真实场景落地”：一边是 Grok 4.5 进入 SpaceX、Tesla 私测，强化大模型与工程制造、自动驾驶等核心业务的结合；另一边是 Plant Talk 和本地端 AI 合作，显示 AI 正向日常环境交互、边缘设备和个人部署延伸。共识在于，多模态、本地推理和企业内部应用会成为下一阶段重要方向，AI 不再只是聊天窗口里的能力展示，而是在进入工作流、设备和物理世界。分歧主要集中在“真实价值还是营销包装”：Grok 的参数规模和对标 Claude Opus 的说法是否可靠，Plant Talk 是实用助手还是拟人化噱头，本地 AI 能否在成本、性能和易用性上挑战云端服务。潜在风险则包括前沿模型能力被夸大、企业私有数据形成封闭优势、NVIDIA 等硬件平台进一步集中生态话语权，以及环境感知型 AI 在隐私、误判和用户过度信任上的问题。

🔹 💡 大佬观点(Influencer Insights)

基于过去24小时内的推文，我为您汇总并提炼了AI行业的关键动态。

📢 AI 行业舆情日报 (基于 X 平台 Influencers 推文)

数据周期: 2026年6月24日 - 2026年6月29日

🔹 1. 今日大佬们共同关注的技术趋势或产品热点

▫️ **趋势一：前沿模型发布方式“政治化”与准入管制**
这是本周社区讨论的最高烈度话题。超级大模型不再是“一键发布”，而是被政府严格管控。
• 🔒 GPT-5.6 的“有限预览”：@dotey 详细分析了 OpenAI 发布的 GPT-5.6（Sol/Terra/Luna），指出模型本身能力极强（Terminal-Bench 2.1 得分超 Claude Mythos 5），但因美国政府要求，目前仅向少数获批伙伴开放，开启了“逐个客户审批”的先例。他引用了 @steph_palazzolo 的报道，称这意味着公司内部拥有的能力和公众能用到的能力的差距会越拉越大。
• ⛓️ Mythos 5 的“部分解禁”：@dotey 同样报道了 Anthropic 的旗舰安全模型 Mythos 5 在被封禁两周后，获美国政府批准向约 100 家关键基础设施机构重新开放。他指出，这一事件标志着“美国政府对前沿 AI 模型的发布前审查，正在从个案变成惯例”。
• 📉 端侧成本压力：@zhixianio 和 @williamlab 关注到苹果因关税/成本问题对产品大幅涨价 20%，感叹这种级别的利润压力对其他厂商而言可能更残酷。

▫️ **趋势二：端侧模型（On-device）与开源小模型的“狂暴测试”**
大佬们对轻量化模型的性能极限有极高关注度，尤其是谷歌 Gemma 系列。
• 🤖 Gemma 4 实测翻车与亮点：@zhixianio 对 Gemma 4 12B Coder 进行了严苛的“一次成型”Vibe Coding 测试（俄罗斯方块、Three.js星系）。结论是 12B 模型依然有天花板，在复杂有状态的长程序生成上明显弱于 Qwen 35B MoE；但不影响 Gemma 4 日文邮件解析等普通任务表现优异。他高度评价 Google 针对端侧的 QAT（量化感知训练）优化思路。
• 📱 音视频交互突破：@zhixianio 测试本地运行 MiniCPM-o 4.5 的全双工音视频，对 9B 模型能达到的效果表示“很满意”，认为虽然有优化空间，但已具备可用性。这体现了社区对“全模态端侧交互”的积极探索。
• 🛠️ Agent 开发基建平民化：@vista8 和 @AI_Jasonyu 均强推腾讯云 EdgeOne Makers，强调其解决了 Agent 从本地 Demo 到上线的部署困境。@vista8 特别指出其“3 行命令部署”、“持久化 Blob 存储”、“沙箱回收”等能力正在利好中小企业。

🔹 2. 值得注意的独特观点或行业前瞻

▫️ **🚀 Claude Tag：LLM 交互的第三次重构？**
这是本周最具影响力的产品哲学讨论。@dotey 引述了 @karpathy 将 Anthropic 的 Claude Tag 定性为 LLM 交互的“第三次重新设计”（从网页版到 App，再到嵌入工作流的持久化异步实体）。他还转述了 @GergelyOrosz 的观点：重点不是 Slack Bot，而是它开箱即用地接入了公司内部系统，对非工程师和新员工的赋能是巨大的范式变化。@dotey 将此总结为 Codex 发展趋势是“Agent OS 而不仅仅是 Agent Office”。

▫️ **👴 算法回归老师傅：AI 幻觉的现实反噬**
@dotey 引用了福特汽车的激进案例：福特因为 AI 质检未达预期，重新雇回了 350 名资深“白须”工程师来调教 AI，并因此重夺新车质量榜第一。他还列举了 Klarna 的 AI 客服质量差、麦当劳撤下 AI 点餐等反例。这与当前“全面替代”的主流叙事形成强烈反差，强调了 AI 产业如今极其缺乏“高质量的领域经验数据” 和人类专家反馈闭环。

▫️ **⚡️ Token 异质性与人机同化**
• 电力 vs. Token：@lijigang 极具启发性地指出，电力是同质的，但 Token 是高度异质的（1M tokens 的 GPT-5.6 跟豆包是完全不同的价值）。这种差异性意味着大模型不会变成普通的水电基建，而更可能走向“征税式”的定价，并形成供给瓶颈。
• 语言的模型味儿：@lijigang 还提到，重度使用某一个模型（如 Claude 或 DeepSeek）会反过来影响人的语言风格，这反映出大脑神经网络非常“吃”上下文。对于开发者而言，这是脑机融合的初级信号。

▫️ **🛡️ “代码护城河”的崩塌**
@ruanyf 转发了黑客新闻的讨论，并坚持他之前的观点：AI 让软件代码本身的护城河迅速消失，只要投入少量算力就能复刻大型项目。这迫使行业将重心从“编写代码”转向“积累难以复刻的高质量测试用例集”。

🔹 3. 推荐的工具或资源

本周推荐高度集中在降本增效的云平台和精细化控制的开源工具上：

1️⃣ 腾讯云 EdgeOne Makers (多位博主推荐):
    • 来源: @vista8, @AI_Jasonyu

SOLO DEV MAKES $48,000 A MONTH FROM A SPACE HORROR GAME HE BUILT WITH CLAUDE, FREE UNITY ASSETS, AND ZERO TEAM

the game looks like iron lung crossed with hardspace shipbreaker. ps1 graphics, red crt warnings, eva spacewalk during a solar flare. sells on steam for $14.99 a copy.

he doesn't run ads. doesn't pay influencers. doesn't have a marketing team. the entire distribution engine is one tiktok account where he posts 51-second clips of the game looking ominous. one clip a week. the steam page does the rest.

the stack guess based on visible artifacts: free unity assets for the station geometry, claude for the systems code, an old gaming pc to render, a phone for the tiktok cuts. probably $0 in software outside steam's revenue share.

the moat isn't art. it isn't gameplay. it's the 51-second loop that converts strangers into buyers at zero marketing cost.

the loop is dumb and reproducible:

→ lo-fi crt aesthetic, ps1-era polygons, scanlines, red overlay
→ one threat-text headline white on black. "don't be outside during a solar flare"
→ red warning text crawl above and below the visual. "magnetosphere breach in sector 7 :: source: solar"
→ HUD with falling stats in the corner. oxygen 71%. safer: false. tether: false.
→ 30-50 seconds. no narration. no gameplay reveal. no logo. just vibe and dread.

studios hire trailer agencies for $80k and 6-month campaigns. this guy films one clip in 20 minutes and clears $48k a month.

the only thing that's still hard in indie gamedev in 2026 is taste. the rest is now solvable from a bedroom.
